clue.text: Snail shell found in wood in valley alongside river

indicators.note: the shell of a word is its outside, so only its first and last letters
the shell is placed inside the valley word

parts.note: a dale is a valley

indicators.note: the river sits next to the rest

parts.note: the shell of WOOD: its first and last letters, placed inside DALE
R = river

explanation.surface: A naturalist finds an empty snail shell in a wooded riverside valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snail' is not the animal here but a slowcoach, someone who moves at a snail's pace; 'shell' reads as the snail's own and is really an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A snail is a figurative name for a slow mover, which is exactly what a dawdler is.

clue.text: Second assignment with upcoming exercise penned

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means reading bottom to top

parts.note: a duty is an assigned task

indicators.note: the exercise is shut inside the assignment

parts.note: PE = physical education, school exercise; turned up to give EP inside DUTY

explanation.surface: A second homework task comes with some exercise to write up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like an adjective or a unit of time, but it is the noun: a second-in-command.
explanation.definitionFit: A second is someone who stands in for or assists another, which is a deputy.

clue.text: See 27 Across
Camouflaged creature, appendage on branch covered by something green

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sits on top of the next
the green thing goes over the top of the rest

parts.note: a lea is a grassy meadow
a fin is an appendage of a fish
a sect is a branch of a religion

explanation.surface: A disguised animal clings to a branch, hidden under green foliage.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a real branch and leaves, which is the leaf insect's habitat; the branch is really a religious offshoot.
explanation.definitionFit: The leaf insect is famous for its camouflage, its body shaped and coloured like a leaf.

clue.text: One number I have in work schedule for hard-working poster girl

indicators.note: the first three pieces go inside the work schedule

parts.note: a roster is a rota of shifts; the rest goes inside it
I = one, the Roman numeral
a number here is something that numbs: ether is an anaesthetic
I've = I have

explanation.surface: A worker has her number and her shifts written into the rota.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is read as a numb-er, something that makes you numb. Rosie the Riveter is the American Second World War poster of a woman factory worker flexing her arm.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosie the Riveter was the wartime poster figure of the hard-working woman in industry.

clue.text: First in steeplechase, barring grey

indicators.note: take the first letter of the next word

parts.note: the first letter of steeplechase
barring = unless, as in 'barring accidents'

explanation.surface: A racing tipster's line: this horse wins the steeplechase unless the grey beats it.
explanation.walkthrough: In racing a grey is a horse's colour, so 'grey' looks like a runner; here it describes the weather.
explanation.definitionFit: A grey day is overcast, one without sun.

clue.text: Poison to drink? Drunk's a bit keen!

indicators.note: drunk letters are scrambled

parts.note: the S of the apostrophe-s is used as a letter; nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone who has had too much warns that the drink is poison, which shows how keen they have been.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's looks like part of 'Drunk's' but is lifted off to join the letters. Snakebite is a British pub drink of lager and cider, notorious for its strength.
explanation.definitionFit: A snakebite injects poison, and snakebite is also a drink, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Gas one's lit under bottom of saucepan

indicators.note: in a down answer, what comes under sits after the first piece
in a down clue the bottom of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the bottom, or last letter, of saucepan is N

indicators.note: lit is slang for drunk, and drunken letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone lights the gas ring below a saucepan.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is': one is lit, so ONE is rearranged to EON and placed under N, the last letter of 'saucepan'.
explanation.definitionFit: Neon is one of the noble gases, the one that glows in advertising signs.

clue.text: Cross on temple discovered in possession of listener, ideal

indicators.note: the ear holds the other letters, as if owning them

parts.note: a listener is an ear, the organ that hears

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another comes above it

parts.note: X is the shape of a cross

indicators.note: dis-covered means stripped of its covering, so the outer letters of temple go

parts.note: temple with its first and last letters removed leaves EMPL

explanation.surface: Someone describes an ideal person as having a cross tattooed on the temple, near the ear.
explanation.walkthrough: TEMPLE without its outer letters is EMPL; X goes on top of it, and the ear contains both.
explanation.definitionFit: An exemplar is a model or perfect example to copy, so as a noun it means an ideal.

clue.text: Famine in southern Detroit?

parts.note: S = southern
Detroit is the capital of the American car industry: a car city, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: A headline asks whether there is famine in the south of Detroit.
explanation.walkthrough: Detroit is not a definition by example but the wordplay: its nickname Motor City gives the idea of a car city.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a famine, a dearth of food, is the extreme case of something being in short supply.

clue.text: Five bedded in group, and assassin shoots lover?

indicators.note: five letters lie bedded in the words that follow

parts.note: grouP AND Assassin

explanation.surface: A gang is joined by a hitman who shoots his lover.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the old punctuation gag: a panda eats shoots and leaves, while an assassin eats, shoots and leaves. Here shoots are bamboo shoots.
explanation.definitionFit: Pandas live on bamboo shoots, so a panda is a lover of shoots.

clue.text: Hence, a time for commercial music programme

parts.note: hence = so, therefore
as printed
pop is commercial music
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A radio schedule has a slot for commercial music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial music programme' looks like a single phrase; the definition is the last word only. The pieces are the time for pop, the pop era.
explanation.definitionFit: A soap opera is a serial television or radio programme.

clue.text: See 4 Down
Pachyderm's head found buried in ice: that's woolly mammoth!

indicators.note: one letter is found sunk inside the other word
woolly means confused or fuzzy, so the letters are muddled
a word's head is its first letter

parts.note: the head of pachyderm is its first letter, P

explanation.surface: An elephant-like beast is found frozen in ice: a woolly mammoth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woolly mammoth' looks like one phrase; 'woolly' is the anagram signal on ICE, giving EIC, and 'mammoth' alone is the definition. P, the head of 'Pachyderm', is found buried in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mammoth and epic describe something on a huge scale, as an adjective meaning enormous.

clue.text: With minimum of warmth, plant grew — did it?

definitions.text: With minimum of warmth, plant grew — did it?

indicators.note: the smallest part of a word, its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of warmth
to plant a body is to inter it
rose = grew, went up

explanation.surface: A gardener wonders whether a plant really grew with so little warmth.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: a winter rose is a hellebore, which flowers in the cold. 'Plant' looks like a noun but is the verb, to bury.
explanation.definitionFit: The winter rose is a plant that grows and flowers with almost no warmth, in the depths of winter.

clue.text: After initial, should I be able to add her partner?

indicators.note: the rest follows the word for initial

parts.note: to initial a document is to sign it
should I be able = if I can
to tot up is to add
as printed

explanation.surface: A man wonders whether, once he has signed, he can add his partner to the form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initial' looks like a noun, a first letter, but is the verb to initial, sign.
explanation.definitionFit: A significant other is a spouse or long-term partner.

clue.text: Dope attending university in Cambridgeshire city, as a matter of fact

parts.note: dope and gen are both slang for information
U = university, placed next to GEN
as printed
Ely is a small cathedral city in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: A drug-taking student at Cambridge, which is simply the truth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' suggests drugs or a fool; here it is slang for inside information, like gen.
explanation.definitionFit: Genuinely and as a matter of fact both mean truly, in reality.

clue.text: Type left disheartened at home, sadly

indicators.note: the letters are arranged badly
the heart of the word is removed, leaving its outer letters

parts.note: LEFT minus its middle
six letters to scramble with LT

explanation.surface: Someone is left alone and miserable at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type' looks like a word for a kind of person; it is printing type. Hot metal is the old method of casting type from molten lead.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot metal is type cast from molten metal, as in old newspaper printing.

clue.text: Elaborate nude seemingly?

definitions.meaning: a verb here: to develop an outline by adding detail
read literally: skin on display, as on a naked figure

explanation.surface: An artist is asked to work up a nude, or so it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a playful reading of the phrase, flagged by the question mark: flesh out on display.
explanation.definitionFit: To flesh out is to elaborate, adding substance to an outline.

clue.text: Where link sought for chain on new cycle, not broken by friction ultimately

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are split open by another letter
new suggests the letters are made over in a fresh order
ultimately points to the last letter of the word

parts.note: the last letter of friction is N

explanation.surface: A cyclist looks for a missing link to fix a bike chain after friction has snapped it.
explanation.walkthrough: The bike-chain picture hides the definition: the 'link' is a connection between ideas, sought on Only Connect, a BBC quiz in which teams find what joins a set of clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Only Connect is a television quiz whose contestants look for the hidden connection joining a series of clues.

clue.text: In-jokes, murder

parts.note: wit is clever joking
a hit is a contract murder

explanation.surface: An in-joke about murder, like a crime writers' private gag.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen joins 'In' to 'jokes' to make in-jokes, but 'In' stands alone as the definition: fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in slang: both mean fashionable and up to date.

clue.text: Ending on foot, dropped brick brings frightful feeling?

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the last letter of foot
to drop a brick is British slang for a blunder, an error

explanation.surface: Dropping a brick on your foot gives you a horrible feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: The brick seems to land on a foot; 'dropping a brick' is a British idiom for making a tactless mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: Terror is a feeling of fright, with the question mark acknowledging the play on frightful.

clue.text: Network where I must learn to keep my mouth shut!

parts.note: I, when it is the one acted on, becomes me

parts.words: must learn to keep my mouth shut!
parts.note: the lesson is 'sh!', be quiet

explanation.surface: Someone at work confesses that they need to stop talking.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the wordplay as 'for me, sh!': the person talking is ME and the lesson is SH.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a network of crossing threads with gaps between is a net, which is what the answer names.

clue.text: Limit of growth capital invested in magazine

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it

parts.note: Time, the American news magazine; the capital goes inside it
Berlin is the German capital

explanation.surface: A financial journalist reports that growth capital in a magazine has hit its limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Growth capital' reads as a finance term, and 'invested' keeps up the money theme; the growth is trees and the capital a city.
explanation.definitionFit: The timberline is the altitude above which trees cannot grow.

clue.text: Sweet, shell with new filling

parts.note: an artillery shell is a bomb

indicators.note: the filling of a word is its middle letter

parts.note: the middle letter of new

explanation.surface: A pastry case or shell is given a new filling for pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet' is the British word for a dessert. A bombe is a dome-shaped frozen pudding, and 'shell' and 'filling' both belong to the kitchen picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A bombe is a moulded frozen dessert, a sweet.

clue.text: Resting, veteran comedy actor

definitions.meaning: not working, the theatrical euphemism for an actor between jobs
Eric, a member of Monty Python

explanation.surface: An old comic actor is between jobs.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves seem to describe the same out-of-work actor; the second is Eric Idle of Monty Python.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle means not working, and Eric Idle is a long-serving comedy actor.

clue.text: City in Europe's mid-Northwest, mid-Northeast proving inaccurate?

indicators.note: the letters are shown to be wrong, so they are rearranged

parts.note: MID and NORTH as printed, with E for east: nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A geography correction: a city is placed in the north-west, not the north-east.
explanation.walkthrough: Trondheim sits in central Norway on the west coast, so 'mid-Northeast' really would be inaccurate: the clue's correction is also its instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Trondheim is a Norwegian city, in the middle of the north-west of Europe.

clue.text: See 14
Fortune, for lucky fellow always at the end, one in the money?

definitions.text: Fortune, for lucky fellow always at the end, one in the money?

indicators.note: the letters go inside the money

parts.note: your lot is your fortune in life
a tenner is a ten-pound note; the next letters go inside it

indicators.note: take the end letter of every word, each time

parts.note: the last letters of foR luckY felloW
I = one

explanation.surface: A fortune always comes in the end to the lucky fellow who is in the money.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a lottery winner is a lucky fellow who comes into a fortune. A tenner is British slang for a ten-pound note.
explanation.definitionFit: A lottery winner is a lucky person who ends up with a fortune, in the money.

clue.text: Victory on back of horse, record for jockey

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the last letter of horse
V = victory, as in the V sign
to enter data is to record it

explanation.surface: A jockey wins on horseback and sets a record.
explanation.walkthrough: The horse-racing picture points at jockeys; an eventer rides in eventing, the combined dressage, cross-country and showjumping competition.
explanation.definitionFit: An eventer is a rider in horse trials, a kind of jockey in the loose sense.
